clue.text: Line from the same source about British political type

parts.note: l = line, as in a line of verse
idem is the Latin citation tag meaning 'the same source as before'
B = British, wrapped inside IDEM ('about')

explanation.walkthrough: IDEM is Latin for 'the same' — footnotes use it to repeat a source just cited. Wrap it round B and out comes a compressed political label, the first of this grid's many squashed-together words.

clue.text: Popular houseplant I set in a pot adapted

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.walkthrough: The fodder hides in plain sight as potting instructions — the surface is a gardener repotting, which is exactly where a houseplant answer hides best.

clue.text: They help people with deliveries after car gets in line, we hear

parts.note: auto = car
queues are lines of people

explanation.walkthrough: Autocues help speakers with the delivery of their lines — nothing to do with parcels. The homophone touches only 'line': queues become CUES.

clue.text: Pay attention about opposing points, namely for novice

parts.note: NB — nota bene, 'note well' — splits around the insertion
east and west, opposite compass points
i.e. = namely

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a debating tip. 'Opposing points' is a classic signal for a compass pair, and NB and IE are both Latin tags worth memorising.

clue.text: Quartet playing best performance? That's made-up propaganda

parts.note: the quartet is the four compass points N, E, W, S, 'playing' together in that order
a peak is a best performance — being at your peak

explanation.walkthrough: Newspeak is the invented propaganda language of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four — and its author is waiting at 23 across. 'Quartet' for the four compass points is a trick worth filing away.

clue.text: Female serving as half of ward sister's replacement

parts.note: the first half of WArd — the RD is dropped
'replacement' redeals the letters of SISTER

explanation.walkthrough: The surface stays on the hospital ward, but 'female serving' means waiting tables. A word's 'replacement' — its letters redealt — is a gentler anagram signal than the usual chaos words.

clue.text: Medic and aged Brit traversing America for TV series

parts.note: doc = medic
old-age pensioner, the standard aged Brit
US, straddled ('traversing') by DOC and OAP

explanation.walkthrough: A docusoap — documentary crossed with soap opera — is another of this grid's blended words. OAP, old-age pensioner, is the crossword's standard Brit of a certain age.

clue.text: Newspaper article began in old-fashioned way

definitions.meaning: the opinion piece that runs opposite a newspaper's editorial page, named for its position
the archaic verb 'ope' means to open, and its past-tense form is how something begun is put in old-fashioned language

explanation.walkthrough: An op-ed sits opposite the editorial page — that's where the name comes from. 'Ope' is poetic old English for open, and a meeting that opens has begun.

clue.text: Negative reactions from pedant and his sort, primarily

parts.note: first letters ('primarily') of Pedant And His Sort

explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' points at first letters, and the pedant's own initials spell out his little snorts of contempt — pah! The fodder suits the answer beautifully.

clue.text: Current controller leading party is eccentric

parts.note: a weir controls a river's current — not electricity
a do = a party, a bit of a do

explanation.walkthrough: The 'current' is a river's, not a wire's — a weir holds it back. DO for 'party' is core crossword vocabulary, and here 'eccentric' is a noun.

clue.text: Foci then shifted to computer applications etc

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.walkthrough: Infotech squeezes information and technology into one word, like so many answers in this grid. The stray mark after 'etc' is the Guardian's typo, not a clue.

clue.text: Piece of luggage left on board by guy you heard consuming drink

parts.note: port is the left side when you're on board ship
man = guy
the letter U is said exactly like 'you'
TEA is swallowed ('consuming') by MAN + U

explanation.walkthrough: Portmanteau — Lewis Carroll's word for two meanings packed into one case — is this puzzle's theme named in a single answer. On board ship, left is always PORT.

clue.text: Suspenseful part in capture

parts.note: nailing = capturing; it opens up around BIT
a bit = a part

explanation.walkthrough: To nail a culprit is to capture them, and the clue needs that verb sense rather than the hammer. 'Suspenseful' is the whole definition — one word doing honest work.

clue.text: Concluding pieces from head of state in last literary event

parts.note: coming last is doing worst; DFE slots inside
the concluding pieces — last letters — of heaD, oF and statE

explanation.walkthrough: 'Concluding pieces from' harvests the last letters of all three words that follow, even little 'of'. A wordfest — word plus festival — keeps the grid's blended-word theme running.

clue.text: Drama as seen from the box

definitions.text: Drama as seen from the box

parts.note: the box = the telly, TELE for short
a play = a drama, following TELE

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition — a teleplay is exactly drama seen on the box — while TELE and PLAY rebuild it, so every word earns its keep twice.

clue.text: Weapon, for instance, deployed in unending attack

parts.note: ASSAIL (attack) 'unending' — its final L is dropped
e.g. = for instance

explanation.walkthrough: An assegai is a slender African throwing spear — an obscure answer, so the wordplay is generous. 'Unending' clips the tail off ASSAIL before EG is deployed inside.

clue.text: Proceeds clumsily with talk about growth and height

parts.note: gas = idle talk; it wraps 'about' the rest
a lump = a growth
h = height, as on measurements

explanation.walkthrough: To galumph — Lewis Carroll's blend of gallop and triumph, from Jabberwocky — keeps the portmanteau theme going. GAS for 'talk' is standard crossword currency.

clue.text: Coarse fabric making us hurt after short time

parts.note: time cut short: T
the word itself
sore = hurt

explanation.walkthrough: Tussore, a coarse wild silk, may be unfamiliar — the kindly charade makes up for it. 'Short time' cutting TIME down to T is a move you'll meet constantly.

clue.text: Awfully adorable old pet

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.walkthrough: An anagram that behaves like a definition too: a labradoodle — labrador crossed with poodle, another blend — genuinely is an awfully adorable old pet. Brendan picks fodder that tells the truth.

clue.text: Bellowing, losing head, and having a row

parts.note: ROARING (bellowing) loses its head — the R goes

explanation.walkthrough: Two rows: the definition's row rhymes with 'go' — pulling oars — while the surface's shouting match rhymes with 'cow'. Beheading ROARING settles which one you need.

clue.text: Pound's gone out of fashion — that could affect one's view of things

definitions.text: that could affect one's view of things

parts.note: style means fashion, and the L drops out of the middle of that word
£ is written L, from Latin libra — this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' giving L, from the Latin libra behind the £ sign, is everywhere in crosswords. A stye is the eyelid swelling that genuinely does affect your view of things.

clue.text: Legal action that may be taken on by boarder

definitions.meaning: a lawyer takes on a client's dispute to argue it in court

definitions.text: that may be taken on by boarder
definitions.meaning: the suitcase a passenger takes on board

explanation.walkthrough: Two cases: the one a lawyer takes on, and the one a passenger takes on board. 'Boarder' does the misleading — it sounds like a lodger, not a traveller.

clue.text: Fellow in squad raving at me in first half, otherwise in second

parts.note: 'raving' scrambles AT ME into the first half
'otherwise' scrambles the same four letters differently for the second half

explanation.walkthrough: One four-letter scrap, AT ME, is shuffled twice over — 'raving' one way for the front half, 'otherwise' another for the back. Economical fodder, spent twice.

clue.text: One English author or another abridged

parts.note: the word itself, lifted straight into the answer
H G WELLS, another English author, abridged — the final S is cut

explanation.walkthrough: George Orwell is the 'one', H G Wells the 'another', losing his final S. The pair also anchor the grid's theme: Orwell coined NEWSPEAK, sitting at 4 down.

clue.text: Owner of trunk that must be repacked for the plane

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.walkthrough: The trunk belongs to the animal, not the luggage rack — and by lovely economy the fodder is 'the plane' all that repacking was for.

clue.text: Like bad deal, difficult to undo?

definitions.meaning: deal is cheap softwood, and a poor-quality plank of it is riddled with these little woody lumps
a problem tangled up with these is hard to work loose

explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' is timber — pine or fir — not a bargain, and a poor plank is full of knots. The second sense, a knotty problem, shares the same tangled picture.
